subject: Riemann zeros and GUE statistics
headline: The zeros repel exactly as a Gaussian unitary ensemble does — ratio statistic 0.6155 against a finite-sample GUE control of 0.6163, and 12 control standard deviations from Poisson. Computed from scratch, no dependencies.

findings.question: Does the zeta implementation reproduce known values?
findings.answer: the first five zeros to 4.2e-11, on an engine written from scratch with no dependencies
findings.falsifier: the first five zeros are 14.134725, 21.022040, 25.010858, 30.424876, 32.935062 — an implementation that misses them is wrong and knows it
findings.remedy: none — re-run on any change to the zeta engine; the five known zeros are the regression test

findings.question: Are all the zeros in the range actually found?
findings.answer: 202 zeros below t = 400 against a smooth count of 201.6 — no zeros missed
findings.falsifier: a count that drifts from the counting formula means missed or spurious zeros

findings.question: Do the zeros obey the GUE statistics, or Poisson?
findings.answer: ratio statistic 0.6155 against a synthetic GUE control 0.6163 ± 0.0190, and Poisson 0.3810 — 12.3 control standard deviations away
findings.falsifier: a ratio near the Poisson value would mean the zeros do not repel

findings.question: Is the textbook constant the right reference?
findings.answer: no — 0.5307 is the asymptotic GUE value; at 201 spacings the same estimator returns 0.6163 ± 0.0190, so the zeros are compared against a finite-sample control
findings.falsifier: comparing 201 spacings against 0.5307 would report a 4σ failure of a correct computation — which is exactly what the first run did

limitations: This is a numerical verification of a known result (Montgomery 1973; Odlyzko), not a new claim about the zeros.
The range is t < 400 (202 zeros); the statistics converge further up.
Nothing here says the zeros predict anything physical — it says a number-theoretic object has a spectrum with the same statistics as a physical one.
